summary: Extends the BGP Administrative Shutdown and Administrative Reset messages so operators can send a free-form text explanation of up to 255 octets. It updates RFC 4486 and obsoletes RFC 8203.

eli5.summary: When a router closes a connection on purpose, it can leave a longer note explaining why, so the other operator is not left guessing.

questions: how long can a bgp shutdown message be
what changed between rfc 8203 and rfc 9003
subtitle: Lets a BGP router explain, in up to 255 bytes of UTF-8 text, why it is closing a session.

tldr.problem: Correlating a BGP session teardown with a notice sent by email or telephone is troublesome, and the earlier 128-octet limit was too short for multibyte character sets.
tldr.mechanism: A Cease NOTIFICATION with subcode Administrative Shutdown (2) or Administrative Reset (4) may carry a one-octet length and a UTF-8 string of up to 255 octets.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9003 obsoletes RFC 8203 and updates RFC 4486. Receivers log the text, and senders should stay within 128 octets unless the peer is known to support this specification.

today: RFC 9003 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 8203 and updates RFC 4486, and it has not itself been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why a Shutdown Message
sections.content:
It can be troublesome for an operator to match a BGP-4 session teardown in the network with a notice sent by offline means such as email or telephone calls. RFC 9003 updates RFC 4486 by specifying a way to send a short free-form UTF-8 message inside a Cease NOTIFICATION message, telling the peer why the session is being shut down or reset.

The document obsoletes RFC 8203. The differences and their rationale are in Appendix A.
sections.eli5: Instead of a router just hanging up, it can say a few words first, so the other side knows it was on purpose and why.

sections.title: The Shutdown Communication Format
sections.content:
A BGP speaker that ends a session sends a NOTIFICATION with Error Code 6 (Cease) and Error Subcode Administrative Shutdown (2) or Administrative Reset (4). It MAY then include a UTF-8 string, whose contents are at the operator's discretion.

  • Length: an 8-bit field giving the length of the Shutdown Communication in octets. A value of zero means no Shutdown Communication follows.
  • Shutdown Communication: MUST be encoded in UTF-8. It is not NUL terminated, and UTF-8 shortest-form encoding is REQUIRED.

Multibyte characters mean the number of characters will be less than the length value. A receiving speaker MUST NOT interpret invalid UTF-8 sequences. Reporting is implementation specific but SHOULD include methods such as syslog.
sections.eli5: The note has a little label saying how long it is, followed by the words themselves. If the label says zero, there is no note.

sections.title: Using It in Practice
sections.content:
Operators are encouraged to use the Shutdown Communication to give the reason for the shutdown and to include out-of-band reference materials. The RFC's example is [TICKET-1-1438367390] software upgrade; back in 2 hours: a ticket reference meaningful to both sides, a brief reason, and the expected length of the maintenance.

Length matters for compatibility. A speaker implementing RFC 8203 treats a message longer than 128 octets as an error, with a log message as the likely consequence. A speaker that implements neither RFC 8203 nor this specification treats a message of any length as an error, again with a log message as the consequence.

So a message of up to 255 octets MAY be sent if the peer is known to support this specification. Otherwise a message MAY be sent but SHOULD NOT be longer than 128 octets.

A receiver cannot acknowledge that it received and understood a Shutdown Communication, so operators should not rely on it as their sole way of communicating important events.
sections.eli5: Short notes are safe for everyone. Long notes are only for neighbors you know can read them, and you should not count on the note being read.

sections.title: Error Handling
sections.content: If a Shutdown Communication containing an invalid UTF-8 sequence is received, a message indicating this event SHOULD be logged for the operator's attention. The erroneous or malformed text itself MAY be logged in hexdump format.
sections.eli5: If the note is garbled, the router writes in its logbook that it got a garbled note, so a person can look at it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Unicode has a number of security issues, so implementers and operators are advised to read Unicode Technical Report #36. Shortest-form UTF-8 is REQUIRED to guard against the problems it outlines.

Because Shutdown Communications are likely to appear in syslog output, a carefully constructed message might be formatted so that it looks like extra syslog messages. The 255-octet limit may help limit such an attack.

Unless the BGP session uses a transport that provides integrity, the message could be forged; unless it provides confidentiality, it could be snooped. These issues are common to any BGP message. Users should also consider data minimization practices as outlined in Section 6.1 of RFC 6973.
sections.eli5: Anyone could write a fake note or peek at a real one, and a sneaky note could try to look like something else in the logbook. So keep notes short and do not put secrets in them.

sections.title: IANA Actions
sections.content: IANA has referenced this document at the subcodes Administrative Shutdown and Administrative Reset in the 'BGP Cease NOTIFICATION message subcodes' registry, under the 'Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) Parameters' group, in addition to RFC 4486.
sections.eli5: The official list of codes now also points to this document for these two entries.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 8203
sections.content:
The maximum permitted length changed from 128 to 255 octets. Operators in regions that predominantly use multibyte character sets reported that messages with the same meaning as in single-byte languages did not fit in the old limit. The RFC's example: the phrase 'Planned work to add switch to stack. Completion time - 30 minutes' is 65 bytes, while its Russian translation is 139 bytes.

If a message longer than 128 octets reaches a speaker implementing RFC 8203, that speaker brings it to the operator's attention but otherwise processes the NOTIFICATION as normal.
sections.eli5: Some languages need more bytes for the same sentence, like needing a bigger envelope for the same letter. So the envelope was made bigger.
